item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports history perturbations as diagnostics of model dependence. [Scarcelli et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) search for minimal sequence edits that change recommendations, emphasizing discrete, sequence-aware counterfactuals. [Pandey et al. (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27201) benchmark temporal attribution using a separately trained, masking-robust probe; they report stronger faithfulness for gradient-based methods than raw attention. This highlights a key limitation: deletion sensitivity can reflect unfamiliar inputs as well as informative interactions. [CoDeR+ (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3778863) distinguishes demand shifts from noisy fluctuations, motivating checks beyond simply assuming the newest interactions represent intent.\n\nFor this task, a practical synthesis is paired evaluation on identical training-history prefixes: intact history, equal-sized recent versus older deletions, and repeated order shuffles preserving item membership. Keep candidates fixed across each pair; report next-item rank changes, HR@10 differences, and top-10 overlap. Control deletion count, padding, and positional changes; separate shuffling within the recent window from whole-history shuffling. If the architecture includes a recent-interest residual, disable that component separately and measure whether its ranking effect aligns with recent-history sensitivity. Define coherence only from available histories, titles, descriptions, or timestamps. Report paired user-bootstrap confidence intervals separately for all four datasets, clustering multiple prefixes by user. These are proposed diagnostics, not established findings: greater sensitivity to recent coherent items supports model reliance on that evidence, but does not establish causal user intent or prove shortcut learning."}
